title: Yesterday
job: Past tense — the first big divergence
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: Hier + je suis + allé(e) + à + place
Je ne suis pas + allé(e)/resté(e) + à + place

rules.text: The past is TWO words: an auxiliary carrying the person, and a past participle carrying the verb — j'ai mangé. This is the passé composé, and it is French's ORDINARY past: j'ai mangé is "I ate". English's "I have eaten" is only sometimes the same thing, and translating it that way every time would mistranslate the whole module.

Most verbs take avoir as that auxiliary. A short, closed set of movement-and-change verbs takes être instead — aller, venir, partir, arriver, rester — and there is no rule behind the split, only the list.
With être the participle AGREES with the subject: je suis allé for a man, je suis allée for a woman, and the extra -e is silent. With avoir it does not agree at all: j'ai mangé, whoever is speaking.
The negation wraps the AUXILIARY, never the participle: je n'ai pas mangé · je ne suis pas allé. The participle stands outside the brackets, exactly as L1-M3's bare infinitive did.

There is no did. English builds its past question and its past negative out of "do", and French has nothing standing in that slot — the auxiliary it already has does both jobs. Reaching for the wrong auxiliary (j'ai allé) is the same English reflex arriving one step earlier: aller is on être's list.

The accent IS the tense. mange is "I eat" and mangé is "eaten", and they differ by nothing else at all — so the acute goes on every -er participle, every time. Worse for the ear: mangé and the bare form manger are said exactly alike.
ne shortens to n' in front of a vowel and welds onto the verb: je n'ai pas. It is the same shortening that turns je into j', and it makes n'ai a single written word.
hier stands at the front of the sentence or at its end, exactly like L1-M4's time words, and nothing else moves around it.

words.note: yesterday. Its h is silent and behaves like a vowel, so nothing is aspirated and the word begins on the y sound: yair.
avoir, with je welded on: je + ai cannot stand as two vowels, so j'ai. Two jobs — plain possession ("I have"), and the auxiliary that builds the past before a participle. Its vous shape is avez.
the past participle of manger — its own word, not another spelling of L1-M4's mange: mange is "I eat", mangé is "eaten", and the accent is the entire difference. mangé and manger sound exactly alike.

sentences.trap: English's "I have eaten" and "I ate" are two different tenses. French has one shape for both here, and the everyday reading is the simple one: Hier j'ai mangé du pain is "Yesterday I ate bread", not "Yesterday I have eaten bread", which English does not even allow beside "yesterday".
sentences.sound: yair zhay mahn-ZHAY. j'ai is one syllable, and mangé sounds identical to manger — the ending is the same clean ay.

variations.changed: swap what was eaten — the partitive behaves exactly as it does in the present
avez for the person you are speaking to — and English's "did" has nothing to translate into

mistake.why: Without its accent, mange is the present — "I eat". The participle is mangé, and the acute is the only thing that says so.

sentences.usage: The plainest thing anyone says about yesterday.
sentences.mnemonic: Two words for one English one: have + eaten = ate.

words.note: the past participle of boire, and nothing about it can be built from bois: irregular verbs have irregular participles, and this one has to be learned whole. It takes avoir, like almost everything.

sentences.trap: The -er verbs give a participle that looks like the infinitive with an accent. The irregular ones give no warning at all — boire becomes bu, and a learner who reasons from the present will write boiré, which is not a word.
sentences.sound: bü, one tight syllable, the same French u as in du and une. The whole sentence is four beats: yair zhay bü dü ka-FAY.

variations.changed: swap the drink — the participle does not move
avez and a rising voice; the participle is unchanged

variations.display: Je n'ai pas bu de café
variations.changed: the brackets round the auxiliary, and the partitive collapses to de

mistake.why: boire is irregular and its participle is bu. There is no -é form to build here.

sentences.mnemonic: boire is short in the past: bu, and nothing more.

words.note: the past participle of travailler — the regular pattern, the -er of the bare form swapped for -é. Like manger and mangé, the two are said exactly alike: only the page tells them apart.

sentences.trap: This sentence has no object at all, and the participle still does not change. A learner looking for the missing "did" will try to put something in front of the auxiliary; there is nowhere for it to go.
sentences.sound: tra-va-YAY — identical to travailler. The ill is a y as in "yes", and the ending is the same ay as every -er.

variations.display: Hier j'ai travaillé à la maison
variations.changed: a place phrase behind the participle — it does not disturb the pair
avez, a rising voice, and hier moved to the end
the brackets round the auxiliary, with the participle outside them

mistake.why: That is the bare form, not the participle. They sound the same, so the ear is no help — the past takes travaillé, with the accent.

sentences.usage: Saying what you did with a day.
sentences.mnemonic: -er for the bare form, -é for the done one, and no way to hear the difference.

sentences.display: Hier je suis allé à Paris

words.note: the past participle of aller, one of the small set that takes être rather than avoir — the movement verbs: aller, venir, partir, arriver, rester. So it agrees with the subject: je suis allé · allée.

sentences.trap: English uses one auxiliary for everything — "I have eaten", "I have gone". French splits them, and the split is a list rather than a rule: aller is on être's list, so je suis allé, never j'ai allé.
sentences.sound: zhuh swee a-LAY. je suis runs together as one breath, and allé ends on the same ay as every -er participle.

variations.display: Hier je suis allée à Paris
variations.cue: Yesterday I went to Paris (a woman speaking)
variations.changed: the -e because of who is speaking about herself — and nothing changes in the sound
êtes for the person spoken to — être all the way through, and a rising voice

variations.display: Hier Anne est allée à Paris
variations.changed: est for a third person, and the participle follows Anne into the feminine

mistake.why: aller is on être's list, so the auxiliary is suis: je suis allé. English's one auxiliary is what makes avoir look right here.

sentences.mnemonic: If the verb moved you or kept you still, it takes être.

words.note: ne welded onto ai. ne cannot sit next to a vowel, so it shortens to n' and the two become one written word — the shortening that turns je into j'. pas still follows the auxiliary: je n'ai pas mangé.

sentences.trap: English puts its "not" next to the auxiliary and its verb after — "did not eat". French does the same, but with the second half of the negation: the participle stands OUTSIDE the brackets, not inside them.
sentences.sound: zhuh neh pa mahn-ZHAY. n'ai is one syllable, neh, and nothing at all is heard of the apostrophe.

variations.display: Je n'ai pas bu de café
variations.changed: swap the participle, and the partitive collapses to de behind the brackets
avez inside the same brackets, and ne shortens in front of it too
the brackets come away and j'ai comes back whole

mistake.why: pas goes immediately after the AUXILIARY, not after the participle: je n'ai pas mangé.

sentences.usage: Saying what you did not do yesterday.
sentences.mnemonic: The brackets grip the little verb; the big one stays outside.

sentences.display: Je ne suis pas resté à la maison
sentences.literal: I not am not stayed at the house

words.note: the past participle of rester, to stay — the change-of-nothing verb that is nonetheless on être's list — the list is learned, not reasoned. An être verb, so it agrees: je suis resté · restée.

sentences.trap: Here suis is not the auxiliary a learner expects and ne is not shortened, because suis begins with a consonant. Both halves are ordinary, and both look strange after S05.
sentences.sound: res-TAY. The whole line is six beats and only the last one is stressed: zhuh nuh swee pa res-TAY a la meh-ZOHN.

variations.display: Hier je suis resté à la maison
variations.changed: the brackets come away, and hier takes the front

variations.display: Je ne suis pas restée à la maison
variations.cue: I didn't stay at home (a woman speaking)
variations.changed: the -e for a woman — the agreement survives the negation untouched

variations.display: Vous n'êtes pas resté à la maison ?
variations.changed: êtes inside the brackets, and ne shortens in front of its vowel

mistake.display: Je n'ai pas resté à la maison
mistake.why: rester is on être's list, so it is je ne suis pas resté. avoir is the auxiliary English would have picked.

sentences.mnemonic: Staying counts as movement to French — rester is on the être list all the same.

words.note: the past participle of voir, to see — irregular, and as short as bu. The bare form is not taught here; the participle is the shape this module needs.
film — masculine, so le film and un film. It is borrowed from English and said almost the same way, with the i short.

sentences.trap: The article is back to un, not du: a film is one countable thing, so L1-M3's rule decides it and the past tense has no say in the matter.
sentences.sound: vü, the same tight u as bu. film keeps its English shape but nothing of the English l-sound at the end — it is lighter, and the i is short.

variations.changed: a person instead of a thing — a name needs no article at all
avez, a rising voice, and le for one particular film

variations.display: Je n'ai pas vu le film
variations.changed: the brackets round the auxiliary; le survives them, because it is not a partitive

mistake.why: voir gives vu, with nothing left of the middle of the verb. Irregular participles are learned whole.

sentences.mnemonic: boire gives bu, voir gives vu — the short ones are the irregular ones.

words.note: the past participle of acheter, to buy — a regular -er verb, so the participle is the bare form with -é. It takes avoir, and it is the verb L1-M8's shopping will lean on.

sentences.trap: English cannot ask this without "did". French asks it with the auxiliary it already had and a rising voice, and adds nothing whatsoever.
sentences.sound: voo-za-vay ash-TAY. The -s of vous wakes into a z in front of avez, so the first three words run as one.

variations.changed: swap the object — a countable one, so une rather than du
the answer, in the first person, with hier taking the front

variations.display: Vous n'avez pas acheté de pain ?
variations.changed: the brackets round avez, with ne shortened in front of its vowel

mistake.why: Two things: this course asks with a rising voice rather than by inverting, and a question always carries its mark. Vous avez acheté du pain ?

sentences.usage: Asking what someone did — across a kitchen or a counter.
sentences.mnemonic: No "did" anywhere: the auxiliary was already doing that job.

words.note: the past participle of parler, to speak — regular -er again, so the bare form with -é. Like every regular participle, it sounds exactly like the bare form it came from.
with. It behaves like its English twin and needs nothing said about it — except that its final -c IS pronounced, which most final consonants in French are not.

sentences.trap: Nothing here is a trap, and that is worth noticing: avec is a straight transfer, and the past is the shape S01 built. The module's difficulty lives in the auxiliary, not in the vocabulary.
sentences.sound: par-LAY a-VEK. The c of avec is one of the few final consonants French says out loud.

variations.changed: swap the person — nothing else in the sentence moves
avez and a rising voice

variations.display: Je n'ai pas parlé avec Anne
variations.changed: the brackets round the auxiliary; avec Anne stays outside them

mistake.why: The bare form again where the participle belongs. They sound alike, so the accent is the only signal: parlé.

sentences.mnemonic: Regular verbs give up their -er and take an -é, and say nothing about it.

words.note: the past participle of faire, to make or to do — irregular, and one of the most useful words in the language, because faire covers both English verbs at once. It takes avoir. The final -t is silent.

sentences.trap: English splits "make" from "do" and French does not: faire is both, and choosing between them is a decision a French speaker never has to make.
sentences.sound: feh, one syllable, with the final -t silent — it sounds like the -ait of lait.

variations.changed: swap the mass noun — the partitive is unaffected by the past
avez and a rising voice

variations.display: Je n'ai pas fait de café
variations.changed: the brackets round the auxiliary, and du collapses to de behind them

mistake.why: faire is irregular: its participle is fait, and there is no -é form to build.

sentences.usage: Saying what you made or did.
sentences.mnemonic: One verb for make and for do, and one short participle for both: fait.
